landmarks.writeup: A protected rainforest area known for its biodiversity and endemic species.

landmarks.name: Roça Sundy
landmarks.writeup: A historic plantation site linked to the abolition of slavery in the islands.

wiki.extract: Sundy is a settlement in the northwestern part of Príncipe Island in São Tomé and Príncipe. Its population is 416. Sundy lies 5 km northwest of the island capital of Santo António. In 1822 the first cocoa plantation of the whole archipelago was established in Sundy. Several buildings of this plantation have been preserved.

landmarks.name: São Sebastião Museum
landmarks.writeup: A cultural museum housed in a former fortress showcasing local history.

wiki.extract: São Tomé is the capital and largest city of the Central African island country of São Tomé and Príncipe. Its name is Portuguese for "Saint Thomas". Founded in the 15th century, it is one of Africa's oldest colonial cities.

cultural_events.name: São Tomé and Príncipe Independence Day
cultural_events.writeup: Celebrated on July 12, marking independence from Portugal in 1975 with parades and cultural performances.

wiki.extract: Portuguese São Tomé and Príncipe was a colony of the Portuguese Empire from the discovery of the São Tomé and Príncipe islands in 1470 until 1975, when independence was granted by Portugal.

cultural_events.name: Festival of the Black Christ
cultural_events.writeup: A religious and cultural festival featuring processions and traditional music.

food_writeup: The cuisine features seafood, tropical fruits, and dishes like calulu, a stew made with fish or meat, vegetables, and palm oil, reflecting Portuguese and African influences.
brief_history: Discovered by Portuguese explorers in the late 15th century, the islands were uninhabited before colonization. They became a key site for sugar and cocoa plantations using enslaved labor. Sao Tome and Principe gained independence from Portugal in 1975 and has since developed as a small island nation with a focus on agriculture and eco-tourism.

commentary.inflation_management: São Tomé and Príncipe's inflation was tamed by the dobra's peg to the euro (since 2010). It ran at 18-32% in 2006-2008, the series high of 32.0% in 2008, on food and fuel prices and monetary instability. The peg brought it down steadily to 5-8% through the 2010s, and the 2022 global shock pushed it back to 18.1% in 2022 and 21.1% in 2023 before collapsing to a projected 0.9% in 2025, the series low. The euro peg is the anchor of the entire macro framework; without it, a microstate with no exports would have no nominal anchor at all.
commentary.debt_management: São Tomé and Príncipe's debt was among the world's highest before relief: 283.2% of GDP in 2006, the series high. HIPC/MDRI completion in 2007 brought it down to 61.0% by 2008, and it has fluctuated in the 55-105% range since, reaching a projected 55.7% in 2025, the post-relief low. The government borrows concessionally and from Portugal and Taiwan; oil exploration hopes in the Joint Development Zone with Nigeria never materialized into revenues. At 56% of GDP for a microstate with almost no exports, the debt is a permanent constraint, and IMF assessments flag high risk of distress; the economy survives on aid, cocoa, and tourism.

key_events.event: HIPC completion-point relief cut debt from 283.2% to about 61% of GDP.
Dobra pegged to the euro, ending the high-inflation era.
Oil exploration in the Nigeria joint zone yielded no commercial finds; hopes faded.
COVID-19 devastated tourism; debt climbed back above 90% of GDP.
Failed coup attempt (November 2022); political instability persisted.
Inflation projected at 0.9%, the series low, as the peg and weak demand contained prices.

commentary.outlook_next_decade: The base case is continued aid-dependent stagnation with low inflation under the euro peg and debt near 55% of GDP. Upside is limited to tourism and any offshore oil surprise; downside is donor fatigue or another shock to a state with no buffers. Uncertainty is moderate: the peg is credible and politics are democratic, but the economy is too small to generate its own momentum.
commentary.caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
